messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ethan, a 37‑year‑old financial analyst who now lives alone in a modest apartment in Chicago, has been living under the shadow of a traumatic captivity that he endured when a car he was driving at night was hijacked. He tells the therapist that the moment the wheel was seized, the roar of the engine became a distant thud, and he was taken to an abandoned warehouse where he was held for twelve harrowing days. In the dark, cold space he recalls the sound of a child’s cry—a piercing, high‑pitched wail that sliced through the silence—along with the sudden, involuntary feeling of a hug from an unknown man’s hand, which made his heart pound and his eyes scan the shadows for a threat. These auditory triggers, especially the children’s cries and the unexpected physical affection, instantly pulled him into a state of alert at home when he returned to his apartment: he feels on guard even inside his own home, his mind perpetually scanning for danger, a sense that a single misplaced sound could signal imminent harm. The mere possibility of silence or a child’s cry in the hallway sets his senses into a constant state of hypervigilance, and he describes the silence between the doors of his own apartment as a “trap” that forces his attention to focus on every creak and rustle. The threat of danger, whether manifest in a child’s cry or an unexpected hug, forces Ethan to remain in a heightened state of vigilance and to keep his life at a constant state of readiness. The memory of the captivity has a profound effect on Ethan’s sense of safety. When he thinks about the event, he can suddenly smell the metallic tang of cold steel and the faint scent of antiseptic that lingered in the warehouse, an olfactory recall that brings the past into the present with terrifying immediacy. He explains that his memories feel more real and vivid than ordinary recollections, and he often says that the event “seems as if it is happening again.” This vividness fuels his sense of threat: each flash of the memory intensifies his hypervigilance and pushes him to remain awake, fearing that the terror will surface in the night. The same memories also reinforce his negative appraisals. He feels as though he violated his own values by having to surrender control and comply with his captors’ demands; he believes he has been dehumanized, reduced to an object to be moved, and he is convinced that the people responsible have faced no accountability. The vividness of the experience, the sensory detail, and the feeling that it was more real than any ordinary memory create a loop in which the memory’s intensity fuels his sense of threat, and the threat magnifies the memory’s vividness, making it impossible for him to detach. Ethan’s negative appraisals create a feedback cycle that pushes him toward the very triggers that initially alarmed him. He has begun to avoid any situation that might produce the sound of a child crying or a sudden hug, fearing that these moments will resurrect the trauma. His belief that he violated his values makes him over‑react to any perceived violation, such as a brief silence in the hallway or the presence of children in the building, thereby generating new instances of threat and hypervigilance. This avoidance in turn reinforces the triggers because each time he avoids a potentially innocuous stimulus—say, a lullaby from a neighbor’s baby, or the hug of a coworker—he feels that he is missing an opportunity to confront the threat and thereby increases his sense that the threat is present. The threat of being caught in a trigger triggers his hypervigilance; his hypervigilance, in turn, heightens the threat that any moment may bring a trigger. This vicious circle keeps Ethan in a state of alert, prevents him from resting, and deepens his sense that he has become a victim of a system that offers no accountability. After months of sleeping only a few hours a night, of missing client meetings because he would not sit at his desk, and of losing the confidence that once made him a valued analyst, Ethan finally decided to seek help. The most recent trigger—an unexpected lullaby from a baby in the hallway above—sent him into a panic that lasted several days, causing him to miss a crucial presentation to senior management. The incident left him with a sense of loss that his job was slipping away because he could not perform under the weight of his hypervigilance. Ethan now fears that he will never regain his professional standing or his sense of personal safety. Yet he also holds a fragile hope that therapy might help him untangle the loop of triggers, threat, memory, and negative appraisals, and reclaim the quiet nights and the steady confidence that once defined his life.
